extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning mathematical proof techniques and elementary set theory (readers of Hammack's Book of Proof)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standard procedures for proving set inclusions, equalities, and identities (element-chasing, case analysis, algebraic manipulation, Cartesian-product arguments), plus methods for disproving statements (counterexamples, universal negation, contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for direct proof (alternatives available)
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, the direct approach usually yields the most straightforward and easy proof, though occasionally the contrapositive is the most expedient. (You can even prove A ∈ B by contradiction: Assume (a ∈ A) ^ (a ∉ B), and deduce a contradiction.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless stated otherwise, use the direct approach. Keep contrapositive or contradiction in mind as alternate strategies when the direct approach is awkward. (Text explicitly: "In practice, the direct approach usually yields the most straightforward and easy proof, though occasionally the contrapositive is the most expedient.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove A ⊆ B by element-wise assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A ⊆ B, suppose a ∈ A and then show a ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard element-chasing template used throughout examples (e.g., assume a ∈ {x ∈ Z: 18|x} and deduce 6|a so a ∈ {x ∈ Z:6|x}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equality A = B by two inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A = B, prove both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard skeleton: [Prove that A ⊆ B.] [Prove that B ⊆ A.] Therefore A = B. Use the element-wise method for each inclusion (see Example 8.10 and Example 8.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions of union, intersection, power set, Cartesian product to deduce membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the formal definitions (e.g., x ∈ A ∩ B means x ∈ A and x ∈ B; (a,b) ∈ A×B means a ∈ A and b ∈ B; X ∈ P(A) means X ⊆ A) to translate set statements into elementary assertions about elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work element-wise using these definitions to move between set-membership statements and algebraic/logical facts (illustrated in Examples 8.6, 8.7, 8.8, and many others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis for unions / power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: When an element belongs to a union (or to P(A) ∪ P(B)), consider cases coming from the definition of union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 8.8: Suppose X ∈ P(A) ∪ P(B). By union definition either X ⊆ A or X ⊆ B; handle each case separately. You do not need a separate case for "both" when either case already covers it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic manipulation of element properties to show membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Use algebraic facts about elements (e.g., divisibility, congruences, prime factorizations) to deduce membership in number-theoretic sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 18|a implies a = 18c so a = 6(3c) and hence 6|a; combining divisibility by 5 and 7 implies divisibility by 35 via prime factors (Examples 8.5, 8.10). Translate element conditions into algebraic equalities and factor/manipulate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set identities by manipulating membership predicates (chain of equalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show equality by producing a sequence of logical/set-builder equivalences transforming one side into the other (manipulate statements of the form {(x,y): ...}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 8.13 uses logical equivalences (including P = P ∧ P) and rearrangement of conjuncts to convert Ax(B∩C) into (AxB)∩(AxC). This can shorten proofs when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nonempty Cartesian-product argument to deduce factor equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If A×C = B×C and C ≠ ∅, then A = B by picking an element c ∈ C and using (a,c) membership to transfer membership between A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 8.11: to show A ⊆ B, take a ∈ A and choose c ∈ C (since C nonempty) to get (a,c) ∈ A×C = B×C, so a ∈ B; reverse roles for B ⊆ A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use distributive and DeMorgan type laws via element method
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove set algebra laws (distributive, DeMorgan, etc.) by showing element-wise containment in each direction, translating operations to logical connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical approach: assume element on one side, use definitions to derive membership on the other; repeat for the reverse inclusion. Several listed identities (e.g., A×(B∩C)=(A×B)∩(A×C)) are proved this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prove obvious trivial inclusions unless requested
rubrics_metrics.description: Some set relations are transparent (e.g., A ∩ B ⊆ A); the text's viewpoint is that such obvious statements need not be written out as formal proofs unless explicitly asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform quick mental checks to be convinced; only write a formal proof for these when exercises or context require it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove a statement by proving its negation (~P)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a statement P is false, prove its negation ¬P; this establishes the falsity of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-rule introduced at start of Chapter 9: "How to disprove P: Prove ~P." The chosen method to prove ¬P may be direct, contrapositive, or contradiction depending on the form of P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving universally quantified statements: counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove ∀x∈S, P(x), produce an example x∈S for which P(x) is false (a counterexample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: "Produce an example of an x∈S that makes P(x) false." Example 9.1: showing n=11 gives composite value f(11)=11·11, disproving the universal primality claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving conditional statements with counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P(x) ⇒ Q(x), produce x with P(x) true and Q(x) false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline given explicitly: "Produce an example of an x that makes P(x) true and Q(x) false." Example 9.2 constructs sets A,B,C giving a counterexample to A−(B∩C)=(A−B)∩(A−C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving existence statements: prove universal negation
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove ∃x∈S, P(x), prove the negation ∀x∈S, ¬P(x) (typically via direct, contrapositive, or contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 9.3: to disprove 'there exists real x with x^4 < x < x^2' one proves for all real x it is not the case that x^4 < x < x^2, using contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by contradiction (assume statement and derive contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P using contradiction: assume P is true and deduce a contradiction, thereby establishing ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: "Assume P is true, and deduce a contradiction." Example 9.5 duplicates Example 9.3's disproof by assuming existence and deriving impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: When presenting a counterexample, show precisely how it falsifies the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A counterexample must be accompanied by an explanation demonstrating that it makes the original statement false (e.g., show the numerical factorization or membership calculation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when using n=11 to disprove primality of f(n), explicitly show f(11)=11·11. Do not merely state the counterexample without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Venn diagrams as an aid to find or understand counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing Venn diagrams can reveal differing regions and suggest specific elements to place in regions to create counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Example 9.2 the text advises drawing Venn diagrams for A−(B∩C) and (A−B)∩(A−C) to see the mismatch and craft the counterexample.
